blocks.text: We can help you with that

DISCLAIMER: Please note that we are not medical professionals, nor is any of our advice official medical advice. This is simply a summary of what we found to be the most helpful on our own individual journeys. No matter what you read online, always verify with recommendations from certified medical professionals!

Autism signs usually emerge gradually, and are noticeable before age three. Knowing this,parents are the ones uniquely positioned to observe, interact, and recognize signs of autism far earlier than diagnosed with their children (Ozonoff et al., 2009). So, parents should investigate and monitor the development of their child if they are not hitting key milestones (Hutman et al., 2019). Early concerns should be checked out and not dismissed as “just delays”.
In fact, the Canadian Pediatric Society recommends screening for all children before the age of three.

Recognizing early Autistic characteristics can help families and caregivers provide support that fosters growth and well-being. It’s essential to remember that each child is unique, and their expressions of being Autistic may vary greatly. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2020), early signs of Autism include:
Not responding to his/her name by 12 months of age.
Not pointing at objects to show interest by 14 months
Avoiding eye contact or preferring to be alone.
Seems not to respond to sound and may appear deaf.
May regress in development such as losing language and/or proficiency skills.
Flapping their hands, rocking their body, or spinning in circles.
Having unusual and sometimes intense reactions to the way things smell, taste, feel and/or look
During the first three years of life, look for these developmental indicators, which may suggest the need for timely screening and assessment by a qualified healthcare professional:
No big smiles or other warm, joyful expressions by 6 months.
No back-and-forth sharing of sounds, smiles, or other facial expressions by 9 months.
No babbling, lack of response to name and no back-and-forth gestures by 12 months.
No imitation or repeating of meaningful two-word phrase by 24 months.
Regressions in development such as losing language and/or proficiency skills.
Possible Signs of Autism at Any Age

This is where it's crucial to note that each person develops at their own pace. However, if someone you know demonstrates differences in meeting developmental milestones for their age, or you identify a potential need for support, no matter the age, it is important to discuss your observations with a healthcare professional to better understand your situation in full (Hutman et al., 2019). Possible Autistic characteristics at any age include:
Avoiding eye contact or preferring to be alone.
Struggles with understanding other people's feelings.
Remains nonverbal or has delayed language development.
Repeats words or phrases over and over.
Gets upset by minor changes in routine or surroundings.
Performs repetitive behaviors such as flapping, rocking or spinning.
Has unusual and often intense reactions to sounds, smells, tastes, textures, lights and/or colors.

Finally, it's crucial to know that Autistic individuals more commonly experience some health conditions compared to non-autistic individuals. These include but are not limited to:
- asthma
- ezcema
- allergies
- reflux
- gastritis
- seizure disorders
- autoimmune conditions
- ear infections
- respiratory infections
- migraine headaches

If you notice a common occurence of any of the following, make sure to book an assessment with the right professional, and, if noticed, bring these up with them: noticeable ups and downs in behaviour, aggression, covering their ears with their hands, grinding teeth, tantrums, tiptoe walking, self-harming behaviour, sore throats, headaches, ear aches, diarrhea, and/or consitpations.

Missing developmental milestones might cause you to worry; however, missing milestones don't translate to an increased likelihood of being Autistic. Of course, it's always helpful to seek information and guidance if you have questions, and to explore further with a trusted expert.

It's important to know which actions to take once certain indicators are recognized.Trust your instincts, monitor the child’s development, and consult a trusted healthcare provider to discuss your observations. Consider requesting an assessment and, if appropriate, a formal diagnosis from a developmental specialist. Don’t hesitate to seek a second opinion if you feel it would be helpful.
